uncited: Splat Kernels and Footprints define the geometric shape, spatial extent, and weighting function of the primitives used in splatting-based volume rendering.
They solve the problem of how to map 3D volumetric data (voxels, particles, or points) onto a 2D image plane while preserving visual fidelity, handling perspective distortion, and managing aliasing.

This family sets itself apart from basic splatting [Splatting Without the Blur](1157-splatting-without-the-blur.md) by introducing sophisticated mathematical models for the footprint function—such as elliptical Gaussian projections [EWA Splatting](1069-ewa-splatting.md) or polynomial splines [Polynomial and Spline Kernels](9995-polynomial-and-spline-kernels.md)—rather than relying solely on fixed-radius disks.
It differs from [Splat Extent and Projection](1792-splat-extent-and-projection.md) by focusing on the internal density distribution of the footprint rather than just its bounding boundaries.
**Primitive Representation:** The volume is decomposed into primitives.
For perspective projections, the kernel shape may be distorted (e.g., EWA splatting) to account for foreshortening [S6, unofficial][S10, abstract only, unofficial].
**Rasterization:** The transformed primitives are projected onto the 2D image plane.
where $\text{weight}(x,y) = F(x-x_D, y-y_D)$ [S10, abstract only, unofficial].
**Compositing:** Contributions are accumulated to form the final image.
Splatting compositing is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time) [S10, abstract only, unofficial].
The concept of splatting originated in the early 1990s as a method for efficient volume rendering.
The term "splat" refers to the shape of the footprint projected onto the screen.
